summary:
Romania decriminalised same-sex relations and the practice is legal nationwide. Outright International's country overview records that Government Ordinance 137/2000 prohibits discrimination on grounds of sex and sexual orientation, while institutional follow-through on that protection is limited. There is no marriage and no civil-partnership regime: the 2018 referendum to amend the constitution failed on low turnout, and the Orthodox Church has opposed a civil-partnership bill since 2017. LGBTI organisations can register and operate.

Legal gender recognition exists and is court-based. In the Arian Mirzarafie-Ahi case, the Sector 6 Court of Bucharest ordered a new birth certificate reflecting the trans man's UK-recognised identity, and the Bucharest Tribunal rejected the appeals filed by the Cluj civil-status directorates, making the decision definitive in March 2026. ACCEPT Romania announced the outcome on Trans Day of Visibility and urges others who have changed their documents in another European Union member state to pursue transcription in Romania.

The legal anchor is the Court of Justice of the European Union's ruling of October 2024, reported by Reuters, that Romania infringed a transgender man's rights in the Mirzarafie-Ahi case, which concerns recognition of a UK gender recognition certificate in Romania. The ruling builds on the position that member states must transcribe intra-EU legal gender recognition.

A Council of Europe thematic review of January 2023, 'Hate Crimes and Other Hate Motivated Incidents Against LGBTI People in Romania', documents the national report on implementation of Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5, covering the legal and policy framework, applicable European Court of Human Rights case-law and international standards.

Official hostility intensified during 2025. The ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 records that anti-LGBTI rhetoric rose through the presidential campaign: candidate Călin Georgescu declared himself 'against LGBTQ' in February, Prime Minister Ciolacu mocked gender-marker changes, and a Ploiești deputy mayor of AUR made further derogatory announcements. The National Audiovisual Council issued a public warning to B1 TV in August over anti-Pride 'provocation' framing after an ACCEPT complaint.

The ILGA-Europe and partners' submission to the EU 2025 Rule of Law Report, whose Romania chapter was authored by ACCEPT, found that eight of nine country submissions reported smear campaigns, disinformation and hate speech against LGBTI people, and cites the surge in anti-LGBTI narratives during the Romanian election period as the clearest example of rights-impacting rule-of-law erosion.

Public visibility carries visible risk. AP reported in June 2025 that tens of thousands marched on the twentieth anniversary of the Bucharest Pride march amid rising right-wing hostility toward LGBTQ+ Romanians.

The ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024, covering 2023, records that the National Council for Combating Discrimination investigated printing houses that refused to print LGBT and gender-equality materials.
tangentialFactors:
Public opinion runs ahead of the legal framework: the IPSOS PRIDE 2023 survey found that 51% of Romanians agree same-sex families should enjoy legal recognition, even though no partnership statute exists.

March 2024 education-law drafts carried anti-discrimination provisions that drew protests from 13 religious groups and a counter-response from more than 50 organisations, indicating the political cost attached to equality language in legislation.

A FRA-commissioned legal study of February 2008 by Romanița Elena Iordache and Iustina Ionescu maps how Romanian law implemented the EU Employment Directive 2000/78/EC and free-movement rules for LGBT partners, including national anti-discrimination concepts, CNCD enforcement powers and NGO complaints. It is a dated baseline for the protection architecture rather than a current assessment.
localsOnly:
Residents can bring discrimination complaints to the National Council for Combating Discrimination, which holds enforcement powers and receives NGO complaints, as set out in the FRA-commissioned study of the Employment Directive's implementation.

Legal gender recognition for residents runs through Romanian courts rather than an administrative procedure, and the Mirzarafie-Ahi judgment establishes transcription of an EU member state's recognition decision as a route available to those who have already changed documents abroad.

A civil-partnership bill has been pending since 2017 and is opposed by the Orthodox Church; the 2018 constitutional-ban referendum failed on low turnout, leaving the constitutional text unchanged.

LGBTI organisations can register as legal entities, and ACCEPT Romania litigates and complains to regulators on their behalf, as in the complaint that produced the National Audiovisual Council's warning to B1 TV.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not source anything on entry or visa screening, border questioning of gender markers, detention or prison placement rules, or access to gender-affirming healthcare for visitors. Those areas remain unresolved here and should not be read as cleared.

No conviction or penalty figures for hate-motivated violence against LGBTI people are available in this inventory. The Council of Europe thematic review of January 2023 is a national implementation report covering frameworks and case-law, and its enforcement outcomes are not sourced.

Whether the transcription route affirmed in the Mirzarafie-Ahi judgment extends to gender recognition issued outside the European Union, including non-EU certificates, is not addressed by the sources and remains unresolved.

The FRA-commissioned study dates from February 2008 and describes the protection architecture as it stood then; its currency against present practice is not sourced.
